slides.headline: A Bombay lawyer never performed music in public. He's the reason Indian classical music has a written notation at all.
Pandit Vishnu Narayan Bhatkhande died on September 19, 1936
slides.body: Bhatkhande, born in Bombay in 1860, trained as a lawyer - Elphinstone College, a law degree, and practice at the Bombay and Karachi High Courts - before abandoning law to spend decades documenting Hindustani classical music.

slides.headline: He classified 180 ragas into 10 thaats - still the basis of music instruction today.
slides.body: His six-volume Kramik Pustak Malika recorded over 1,850 compositions using a notation system he invented himself, after travelling India to persuade hereditary musicians to share compositions their families had guarded orally for generations.

slides.eyebrow: Why it matters for Viksit Bharat 2047
slides.headline: He promised his father he'd never perform publicly - and never did.
slides.body: He edited his final volumes from his sickbed after a stroke in 1933, working until his death. A student in any Indian music school today who names a raga's thaat is using a system built by a man who kept a promise to stay off the stage.

sources.text: Ramesh Gangolli - Chatura Pandit: V.N. Bhatkhande
